q: How do you say the vowel え?
o: Like the a in "say", with a glide
why: Japanese え is always a short, pure "eh", never "ee".

q: You want to write "kore wa" (this is). Which spelling is right?
why: The topic particle is said wa but written は.

q: What do the two dots ゛ do to か (ka)?
why: Two dots turn k into g: か becomes が.

q: What does the small っ do in きって (postage stamp)?
o: Adds a short pause before the t
why: Small っ is a silent beat: kit-te.

q: おばさん means "aunt". How do you write "grandmother"?
why: Grandmother has a long a: おばあさん, with the extra あ right after ば.

q: Which pair differs only in pitch?
why: あめ is written the same both times; only the melody tells rain from candy.

q: What does ー do in コーヒー?
o: Makes the vowel before it long
why: ー makes the vowel before it last two beats: kōhī.

q: How do シ (shi) and ツ (tsu) differ?
o: シ's short strokes sit on top
シ's short strokes sit on the left, and its long stroke sweeps up
why: シ: strokes on the left, sweeping up. ツ: strokes on top, falling down.

q: Why is McDonald's マクドナルド in Japanese?
o: Katakana has no letter for d
Japanese beats end in a vowel, so the consonants get vowels
why: Japanese beats end in a vowel or ん, so ma-ku-do-na-ru-do has six beats.

q: Which is the right self-introduction?
why: さん goes after other people's names, never your own.

q: What does は do in わたしは がくせいです?
o: It marks the topic: "as for me"
why: は is the topic particle; です is the word for "am / is / are".

q: How do you ask Ms. Sato if she is a teacher?
why: Use her name + さん instead of あなた, and end with か.

q: Which is correct for "this book"?
why: この goes before a noun; これ stands alone.

q: The thing is far from both you and the listener. Which word do you use?
why: あ words point at things far from both people; それ is near the listener.

q: How do you say "Where is it?"
why: どこ is "where"; どれ is "which one", だれ is "who", なん is "what".

q: How do you say 20,000?
why: Japanese counts in ten-thousands: 20,000 is two まん, にまん.

q: How do you say 4:00?
why: Four o'clock is always よじ.

q: Which particle goes after a clock time, as in "at seven"?
why: A clock time takes the time particle に: しちじに.

q: How do you say "my friend"?
why: Owner first, then の, then the thing: わたしの ともだち.

q: Emily is a student. How do you say "I'm a student too"?
why: も replaces は: わたしも.

q: A friend asks about your mother. You say "My mother is a teacher."
why: Your own mother, when you talk to others, is はは, with no さん.

q: Where does the verb go in a Japanese sentence?
why: Japanese puts the verb last: すしを たべます.

q: How do you make たべます (eat) negative?
why: Replace ます with ません.

q: あまり (not much) goes with which verb form?
why: あまり needs a negative verb: あまり のみません.

q: "I eat at a restaurant": which particle goes after レストラン?
why: Where an action happens takes で.

q: Which particle marks where you go?
why: With verbs of going and coming, に or へ marks the destination.

q: How do you say "by train"?
why: The means of travel takes で.

q: Which verb do you use for a dog?
why: People and animals take います.

q: "The book is on the desk." Which particle goes after うえ?
why: Where something is takes に: つくえの うえに.

q: Which is right for "next to the bank"?
why: The thing you measure from comes first, then の, then となり.

q: Which one says "I didn't eat breakfast"?
why: Didn't eat: the negative ません plus the past でした, and the object particle を on あさごはん.

q: How do you say "It wasn't my day off"?
why: The past of じゃないです is じゃなかったです.

q: Which time word takes the time particle に?
why: Days of the week take に; きのう, せんしゅう and きょねん take no particle.

q: A coworker says: どようびに えいがを みませんか。 What is she doing?
o: Asking whether you missed a movie on Saturday
Telling you not to watch the movie
Inviting you to a movie on Saturday
why: ませんか, a negative question, is the usual polite invitation.

q: How do you turn down an invitation politely?
why: Apologize and trail off with ちょっと…; a bare いいえ sounds cold.

q: Someone asks: にくは たべませんか (Don't you eat meat?). You don't. What do you answer?
why: はい agrees with the question as asked: that's right, I don't.

q: How is the first kanji of 日曜日 (Sunday) read?
why: 日曜日 is にちようび: にち at the start, び at the end.

q: Which word means Japanese person?
why: 日本 (Japan) + 人 (person), read にほんじん.

q: Do you have to type kanji in your answers?
o: Only for days of the week
why: Kanji are never required; every answer also accepts kana.

q: The movie was interesting. =
why: An い-adjective drops い and adds かったです for the past.

q: Which is right before a noun?
why: きれい is a な-adjective, so it adds な before a noun.

q: It wasn't good. =
why: いい switches to よ- for its other endings: よくなかったです.

q: I like sushi. =
why: すき is a な-adjective, so the thing you like takes が.

q: Which is the softer way to say you don't like something?
why: すきじゃないです is gentler than きらいです.

q: Emily is good at Japanese. =
why: じょうず works like すき: the skill takes が.

q: Two apples, please. =
why: Thing を, then the number, then ください; ふたつ is the all-purpose counter.

q: Which counter is for pens and bottles?
why: ほん counts long, thin things.

q: How do you say one person?
why: One and two people are ひとり and ふたり.

q: What is the て form of のみます (drink)?
why: み before ます becomes んで: のんで.

q: What is the て form of いきます (go)?
why: いきます is the exception: いって.

q: I got up and ate breakfast. =
why: The first verb takes the て form; the last one carries the past ました.

q: Please wait. =
why: まちます is a u-verb: ち before ます becomes って, then ください.

q: May I sit here? =
why: ても いいですか asks for permission.

q: You want a coworker to close (しめます) the door. What do you say?
why: Asking someone else to do something: て form + ください.

q: I'm married. =
why: A state that is still true: て form + います.

q: Do you know Ms. Sato? — No, I don't. =
why: The negative of しって います is しりません.

q: My mother is cooking now. =
why: An action going on now: て form + います.

q: What is the dictionary form of のみます (drink)?
why: のみます is a u-verb: the み sound changes to む.

q: How do you say "there isn't" in the short form?
why: ある is special: its short negative is just ない.

q: You ask a friend "Are you a student?" casually. Which is right?
why: Casual questions drop か and never end in だ.

q: How do you say "I think it's expensive"?
why: An い-adjective goes straight before と, and おもいます comes last.

q: How do you say "I don't think it's difficult"?
why: The negative goes inside the quote: むずかしくないと おもいます.

q: Which word needs だ before と?
why: ゆうめい is a な-adjective, so it takes だ: ゆうめいだと おもいます.

q: How do you say "the book I bought yesterday"?
why: The describing clause goes before the noun, and "bought" is the past short form かった.

q: What is the past short form of のみます (drink)?
why: The て form is のんで, so the past short form is のんだ.

q: "the cake my mother made" =
why: Inside the clause the maker takes が, and the short form つくった goes right before the noun.

q: "The train is faster than the bus." =
why: より goes after the slower one, the bus: でんしゃは バスより はやいです.

q: Which question word asks "which of the two"?
why: どちら is "which" for a choice between two things.

q: Someone asks: すしと ラーメンと どちらが すきですか。 How do you say "Sushi"?
why: Answer with の ほうが: すしの ほうが すきです.

q: "I'm planning to buy a camera." =
why: つもり follows the dictionary form: かう つもりです.

q: "It got cold." =
why: An い-adjective changes い to く before なります.

q: "I'm not planning to go." =
why: Put the short negative before つもり: いかない つもりです.

q: "I want to eat sushi." =
why: Drop ます and add たいです: たべたいです.

q: "I didn't want to go." =
why: たい changes like an い-adjective: たくなかったです.

q: "I want a new bag." =
why: For a thing, use ほしいです with が.

q: "I've eaten natto." =
why: Experience: past short form + ことが あります.

q: What does いく ことが あります mean?
why: With the dictionary form, the pattern means "there are times when…".

q: "I've never been to Okinawa." =
why: Keep いった, and make the end negative: ありません.

q: Your coworker looks pale. What do you ask?
why: どうしたんですか asks for an explanation of what you notice: "What's wrong?"

q: Which is correct before んです for "I'm a student, you see"?
why: A noun takes な before んです: がくせいなんです.

q: "It's my day off, so…" =
why: A noun takes な before ので: やすみなので.

q: "I have to study." =
why: する → しない → しなければ いけません.

q: "You don't have to come." =
why: くる → こない → こなくても いいです.

q: "You'd better go to the hospital." =
why: Advice: past short form いった + ほうが いいです, and going to a place takes に.
